public_cards.title: Major-scale explanation
public_cards.summary: Understand intervals, octave turn, shape and transposition

authored_public_excerpts.text:
IMPORTANT INTERPRETATION
Moving one fixed scale shape by one fret transposes it. A major is the starting rung, not the key of every rung.
A fixed-key A-major exercise in every neck position requires changing the note layout and is a separate later branch.

MAJOR-SCALE FORMULA
Degrees: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
Intervals: whole - whole - half - whole - whole - whole - half

COMPACT ONE-OCTAVE SHAPE - ROOT FRET R ON LOW E
Low E string: R, R+2               Fingers 2,4
A string:     R-1, R, R+2          Fingers 1,2,4
D string:     R-1, R+1, R+2        Fingers 1,3,4
The four-fret hand frame runs from R-1 through R+2.

CELL AND PICKING RULE
Play degrees 1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8, then 8-7-6-5-4-3-2-1. The octave root is repeated at the turn.
This creates 16 notes, so the next key begins with the same alternate-picking orientation.
D-start: D U D U D U D U | D U D U D U D U
U-start: U D U D U D U D | U D U D U D U D
Do not restart the pick cycle at the scale turn or at the one-fret shift.

NECK ROUTE
UP:   A(5) > Bb(6) > B(7) > C(8) > Db(9) > D(10) > Eb(11) > E(12) > F(13) > Gb(14) > G(15) > Ab(16) > A(17)
DOWN: A(17) > Ab(16) > G(15) > Gb(14) > F(13) > E(12) > Eb(11) > D(10) > Db(9) > C(8) > B(7) > Bb(6) > A(5)

PRACTICE RULE
Use 3-4 neighboring rungs at first. Play even eighth notes and pause one beat after every 16-note cell.
During the pause, release pressure and move the complete frame one fret. Repeat with both pick starts.
Then remove the pause, connect the ladder, reverse at fret 17, and return to fret 5.
Add 2 BPM after three clean round trips. Reduce 4-6 BPM after two errors, dragged shift noise, or rising tension.
Advance after the complete route is clean with both pick starts on two separate days.

PURPOSE
Keep the complete A-major-pentatonic neck map from Levels 30-38, rename every note from the viewpoint of F# minor, and make F# sound like home through drone, accent, phrase ending, and repetition. No new fret or pitch is added.

SHARED PITCH POOL
A major pentatonic:  A B C# E F#   = 1 2 3 5 6
F# minor pentatonic: F# A B C# E   = 1 b3 4 5 b7
Pitch-role map:
  A   A major  1   |   F# minor b3
  B   A major  2   |   F# minor  4
  C#  A major  3   |   F# minor  5
  E   A major  5   |   F# minor b7
  F#  A major  6   |   F# minor  1

POSITION LABEL RULE
P1-P5 remain the established Level 34 ascending-neck labels. Do not renumber the boxes. The tonal center changes; the fret map and position identities do not.

F# ROOT ATLAS
Low E 14 | A 9 | D 4 and 16 | G 11 | B 7 | high e 14
P5 is the strongest tonic frame because it begins on low-E fret 14, F#.

========================================================================================================================
MODULE A - A-DRONE / F#-DRONE COMPARISON
========================================================================================================================
Play every eight-note phrase once over A and once over F#. Keep the notes, fingering, rhythm, articulation, and dynamics unchanged.
Shared note contour: B C# E F# A F# E C#

F#m|4---5---b7--1---b3--1---b7--5---|
Fng|1---3---2---4---2---4---2---3---|

  G|4---6-----------------------6---|
  D|--------------------------------|

MODULE G - RANDOM-CENTER EAR TEST
========================================================================================================================
Cover the answers. Play every five-note card twice and identify the more convincing tonic before checking.

public_cards.title: Blues rhythm/technique legend
public_cards.summary: Read picked/sounding/held/rest/color roles and assess full capstone

authored_public_excerpts.text:
PURPOSE
Combine the A-minor-pentatonic map, the flat-five blue note, shuffle rhythm, A7-D7-E7 chord targets,
major/minor color control, articulation, position movement, motif development, and deliberate space into
complete musical conversations. The objective is not to play more notes. The objective is to make the form,
the active chord, the motif, the phrase boundary, and the dynamic direction audible without losing the pulse.

PITCH POOLS
A minor pentatonic: A C D E G          degrees 1 b3 4 5 b7
A blues scale:        A C D Eb E G       adds b5
A major pentatonic:   A B C# E F#       degrees 1 2 3 5 6
Completion tone:      G# may appear as the third of E7. F may appear only as a marked chromatic approach.

TWELVE-BAR FORM
| A7 | A7 | A7 | A7 |
| D7 | D7 | A7 | A7 |
| E7 | D7 | A7 | E7 |

PHRASE GRAMMAR
A call states a rhythm, contour, register, color, or articulation and leaves a question. A response preserves
at least one recognizable feature while changing the chord target, contour, register, density, or ending.
Silence is counted. A position shift must sound like part of the sentence. The strongest target should arrive
because the harmony changed, not because the phrase ran out of notes.

TAB LEGEND
P = picked attack; h = hammer-on; p = pull-off; s = slide arrival; b = bend; b< = blue-third shade;
r = rest; = = held tone. Color row: C common anchor, m minor-only, b5 blue note, M major-only, * completion.

RECORD-AND-REVIEW RUBRIC - SCORE EACH 0, 1, OR 2
Form awareness: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Rhythmic space: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Chord targeting: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Bend and slide intonation: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Motif continuity: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Position movement: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Dynamic shape: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Recovery after an error: 0 absent / 1 inconsistent / 2 controlled.
Maximum 16. Section-completion standard: 13 or higher on two separate days, with no zero in form awareness,
chord targeting, or recovery.

PRACTICE PROGRESSION
1. Clap the call-and-response rhythms and count every rest.
2. Complete all five local pairs; exaggerate the phrase boundary.
3. Play all four seam conversations and verify every beat-one target.
4. Transform the seed motif in seven ways without changing tempo.
5. Perform sparse, medium, and dense passes at one BPM.
6. Perform the three dynamic-shape exercises without changing subdivision.
7. Learn each model chorus in four-bar blocks, then play all twelve bars.
8. Replace one response bar at a time while preserving the written calls.
9. Practice tonic closes and E7 re-entries until bar 12 has a clear purpose.
10. Record the three-chorus capstone, score it, repair one category, and record again.

MASTERY GATE - SECTION V COMPLETE
Perform all five local pairs and four seam conversations; transform one motif in seven ways; preserve targets
through sparse, medium, and dense passes; play all three model choruses; execute both a tonic ending and a
functional turnaround; recover from a deliberate wrong note without stopping; record three connected choruses
on two separate days; make the A7-D7-E7 form audible without accompaniment; and score at least 13/16.

public_cards.title: Keep the phrase and its pulse in view
public_cards.summary: Understand pulse unit, common-cycle span and beat-four return
paragraphs: In these Level 74 examples, a beat is a quarter note. Count the four beats of the phrase steadily; the upper pattern fits inside that counted span. The ratio describes the two pulse counts over their common span, not a new tempo or a change of meter.

For 3:2, fit three evenly spaced upper pulses across two quarter-note beats while the lower part marks those two beats. The source repeats that two-beat pattern twice to fill its four-beat phrase. The parts meet at the start, again at beat 3, and at the next phrase boundary.

For 4:3, fit four evenly spaced upper pulses across beats 1–3 while the lower part marks those three beats. Beat 4 is the separately written root resolution. Keep that fourth beat: do not stretch the 4:3 span across the entire bar or start another complete 4:3 pattern there.

The tables measure elapsed quarter-note beats from the start: 0 is beat 1, 1 is beat 2, 2 is beat 3, and 3 is beat 4. A value of 4 is the next phrase boundary, not an extra attack in the current phrase. These positions explain alignment; they do not add durations, articulations or performance results.

An accent group running across a 4/4 sixteenth grid is a different construction. The bar has 16 slots; grouping those slots in threes, fives or sevens moves the perceived accent without moving the barline. A group and a bar start together again after 48, 80 or 112 slots: respectively 3, 5 or 7 bars, with 16 groups in each case.

Keep the source studies of 5/4, 7/8, quintuplet and septuplet subdivisions distinct. This bridge does not replace those studies, prescribe a Freeplay configuration, or set a timing tolerance. Use the original source for the notes, fingerboard positions, instructions and full capstone.
3:2 explanatory elapsed quarter-beat alignment: lower 0, 1, 2, 3; upper 0, 2/3, 4/3, 2, 8/3, 10/3.
4:3 explanatory elapsed quarter-beat alignment: lower 0, 1, 2; upper 0, 3/4, 3/2, 9/4.

authored_public_excerpts.text:
PURPOSE
Change the perceived rhythmic center without losing the meter, barline, harmony, or pulse. Train groups of 3, 5, and 7 over the sixteen-note 4/4 grid; metric displacement; quintuplet and septuplet subdivisions; 3:2 and 4:3 polyrhythms; 5/4 and 7/8; and full-form harmonic application.

CORE ARITHMETIC
4/4 contains 16 sixteenth-note slots per bar.
Group of 3 returns after 48 slots = 3 bars = 16 groups.
Group of 5 returns after 80 slots = 5 bars = 16 groups.
Group of 7 returns after 112 slots = 7 bars = 16 groups.

Guitar Exercises - Section X, Level 74
Odd rhythmic groupings, cross-bar accent cycles, metric displacement, and polyrhythmic phrase control
8 MODULES  |  1168 NOTATED CONTACTS
Level 73 changed key centers while preserving phrase identity. Level 74 changes the perceived rhythmic center while preserving the meter, barline, harmony, and pulse. The player
must distinguish a grouping from a meter change, an accent from an extra attack, and a displaced phrase from a lost beat.
1. Keep the meter fixed
A 3-, 5-, or 7-note grouping can cross barlines while the
4/4 measure remains unchanged.
2. Move the accent, not the clock
The accent cycle may drift through every sixteenth slot.
The quarter-note pulse must remain steady.
3. Separate the voices
Polyrhythmic cells assign different pulses to bass and
upper voices without adding or removing time.
Core arithmetic: 16 sixteenth notes per 4/4 bar
GROUP OF 3:  LCM(16,3) = 48 slots  = 3 bars  = 16 groups
GROUP OF 5:  LCM(16,5) = 80 slots  = 5 bars  = 16 groups
GROUP OF 7:  LCM(16,7) = 112 slots = 7 bars  = 16 groups
The barline stays fixed. The accent returns to beat 1 only after the full cycle.
METRIC DISPLACEMENT:
same notes + same rhythm + different starting subdivision
POLYRHYTHM:
two simultaneous pulse organizations sharing one time span
Written workload
Module
Contacts
A - accent cycles
240
B - displacement
64
C - odd subdivisions
192
D - polyrhythms
108
E - odd meters
108
F - harmonic cycles

200
TOTAL
1168
Session protocol
Clap and count first. Next play one muted string. Then play one note. Add the pitch cell only after the accent cycle is stable. During polyrhythms, isolate each voice before combining them. A
wrong note may be repaired inside the form; a lost pulse requires a restart.
ACCENT RULE
An accent changes volume or articulation. It does not create another attack.
Standard tuning. Rhythm-first workbook: grouping, displacement, polyrhythm, and asymmetrical meter.

KEY CHANGE TOO WEAK: lengthen the destination dominant and tonic.
PIVOT SOUNDS RANDOM: state both Roman-numeral functions before playing.
COMMON TONE LOST: sustain or repeat it through the barline.
MELODY SOUNDS RESTARTED: preserve motif rhythm and contour.
VOICE LEAP TOO LARGE: choose another octave or inversion.
SOURCE KEY RETURNS: avoid source-only tones after destination V-I.

- Transpose all six motifs without changing rhythm or scale-degree contour.
- Perform the four eight-bar studies and the sixteen-bar capstone from memory.
- Recover from all twelve weak-note cards without stopping the form.
- Record one related-key and one chromatic-mediant modulation on two separate days.

Section X completion gate and next-stage integration map
SECTION X COMPLETE WHEN PERFORMANCE IS REPEATABLE
ADVANCED INTEGRATION MEANS SYSTEMS SURVIVE CONTACT WITH A COMPLETE PERFORMANCE
Section X mastery gate
Recall 48-bar form from memory
Pre-hear all modulation targets

Recover from one planted error

What Section X has added
The player can now analyze and reconstruct repertoire, hear functional harmony, pre-hear guide tones, navigate modulations, use odd rhythmic groupings without losing the barline, respond to ensemble
cues, switch accompaniment and lead roles, and preserve a complete performance through errors.
This is the point where future material should become less like isolated vocabulary acquisition and more like specialization: repertoire, genre-specific articulation, advanced chord melody, composition,
arrangement, sight reading, or higher-speed mechanics can now be layered onto an integrated musical system.

accompaniment/lead execution.
